content: The standards for outcome measures in an HIV case surveillance system are designed for robust and mature systems. Surveillance systems that are not fully implemented or have not been operational for a sufficient number of years may not meet these standards. However, data from such systems can still be used, provided that routine evaluations of the surveillance system guide decisions on when and what data can be disseminated. Surveillance programs must identify, quantify, and describe the limitations of the data and how these limitations affect the interpretation of analyses. Completeness of Case Ascertainment (Sensitivity): The completeness of case reporting, also referred to as the sensitivity of the surveillance system, is determined by the proportion of all cases reported to the surveillance program that meet the surveillance case definition. Completeness can be measured in three ways: 1. Case-finding exercises: These involve expanded methods to identify cases missed by the surveillance system. For example, reviewing laboratory registers or files to identify individuals with positive HIV antibody or RNA tests. Personal identifying data such as names and dates of birth are collected and compared to cases in the surveillance database. Records not found in the database (missed or newly identified cases) should be fully investigated and reported. This method measures both the completeness of reporting and identifies new cases. 2. Capture-recapture analysis: This method estimates the completeness of reporting in document-based data systems but does not identify missed cases. It assumes that all reports in the surveillance database represent the entire universe of cases and that reporting from one source is independent of reporting from another. Completeness is calculated by comparing cases reported from multiple sources, such as HIV testing programs, care clinics, and laboratories. 3. Comparison of reported cases to expected cases: The expected number of cases should be derived from reliable sources, such as direct laboratory reporting. Discrepancies between reported and expected cases should prompt investigations to address potential issues, such as changes in facility personnel or reduced access to testing kits or antiretroviral therapy (ART). Completeness should be measured 12 months after the end of a calendar year to account for reporting delays and is expressed as a percentage. The minimum performance standard is that at least 85% of expected cases should be reported within 12 months. Timeliness: Timeliness refers to how soon after an HIV diagnosis the patient is reported to the surveillance program. It is calculated as the time from diagnosis to receipt of the case report by the surveillance program. Timeliness can be measured as the median time between diagnosis and reporting or as the proportion of cases reported within a specified time period after diagnosis. Timeliness should be assessed alongside completeness, as incomplete reporting can lead to an overestimation of timeliness. Timeliness should only be measured if reporting completeness is at least 85%. The minimum performance standard is that at least 66% of cases in a calendar year should be reported within six months of diagnosis. Accuracy: Accuracy refers to the correctness of the data reported to the surveillance program. It is measured by re-abstracting data from a sample of reported cases and comparing it to the data in the surveillance database. Discrepancies should be identified and reconciled, with the correct data retained in the database. Re-abstraction should be performed by someone other than the person who completed the original report and should occur within 12 months of the case being reported. Sentinel events occurring after the case was reported should be collected but not factored into the measurement of data accuracy. The evaluation of accuracy can be conducted nationally, subnationally, at the facility level, or for individual surveillance officers. Results must be reported back to healthcare providers, surveillance staff, and others involved in case reporting to improve methods and data quality. Outcome measures should be tracked over time to monitor changes in performance. The minimum performance standard for accuracy is that at least 85% of required reporting variables are correct compared to re-abstracted data. In settings with electronic medical records submitted directly to the surveillance program, measuring accuracy may not be necessary. However, if data are transcribed from paper medical records into electronic systems, the accuracy of the information reported to surveillance must be evaluated using the paper record as the primary source document. Sampling for re-abstraction may involve random sampling or a two-stage strategy, considering factors such as the number of diagnosed cases, reporting facilities, and available resources. In most programs, a re-abstraction sample of 5–10% is sufficient, but in areas with fewer than 100 reported cases, all cases should be re-abstracted. At a minimum, variables required to count a case for surveillance purposes, such as the patient’s name, date of birth, sex, date of diagnosis, clinical stage, CD4 test result, and date of death (if applicable), should be validated. Additional variables, such as ART initiation date and viral load test results, should be abstracted if feasible.
